solution.concept_anchor: CCIL membership eligibility categories
solution.strong_distractor: b — 'Insurance companies' as a CCIL member category is less commonly known than banks or primary dealers, making candidates who are uncertain about insurance companies' eligibility likely to mark them as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Recall CCIL membership categories: banks, primary dealers, insurance companies, and select RBI/SEBI-regulated financial institutions meeting net worth criteria.
Evaluate option (a) — Scheduled Commercial Banks: Core CCIL members — they hold G-Secs and participate in forex and money markets. Eligible.
Evaluate option (b) — Life Insurance Companies: LIC is a promoter of CCIL and insurance companies are eligible members participating in G-Sec markets. Eligible.
Evaluate option (c) — Primary Dealers: These are market makers in G-Secs and among the most active CCIL members. Eligible.

Evaluate option (d) — Non-Banking Financial Companies (as a general category): General NBFCs do not qualify for CCIL membership — CCIL membership is restricted to specifically regulated entities. NBFCs as a broad category are the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap replaces the ineligible category with one that sounds similar to eligible members. NBFCs are regulated financial entities under RBI, which may lead candidates to assume they qualify for CCIL membership alongside banks. However, CCIL membership is confined to specifically enumerated wholesale institutions — general NBFCs are not among the eligible categories, even though they may participate in money markets through member banks as intermediaries.
solution.final_explanation:
CCIL is a wholesale market infrastructure — its membership is tightly restricted to entities that directly participate in G-Sec, forex, and money markets at an institutional level.

• Option (a) — Scheduled Commercial Banks: Eligible CCIL members — they are the primary participants in all segments CCIL clears.
• Option (b) — Life Insurance Companies: Eligible. Insurance companies are significant G-Sec holders and CCIL members — LIC itself is a CCIL promoter.
• Option (c) — Primary Dealers (PDs): Eligible and among the most active CCIL members. PDs are market makers in G-Secs and have a mandatory role in primary G-Sec auctions.
• Option (d) — Non-Banking Financial Companies (general category): Not eligible for direct CCIL membership as a general category. NBFCs that wish to participate in G-Sec or money markets do so through member banks as intermediaries. Certain select NBFCs with specific RBI designations may qualify, but 'NBFCs as a general category' are excluded — making this the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• Membership criteria include minimum net worth requirements that vary by segment.
• Primary Dealers include both bank-PDs (banking subsidiaries) and standalone PDs — both are CCIL-eligible.

R (CCIL being the only onshore forex CCP) is true, and A (PFMI compliance) is true — but R explains A only through a long inferential chain that does not hold directly. PFMI compliance is mandated by SIFMI designation under RBI's regulatory framework, which applies to all systemically important FMIs — not specifically because CCIL is the 'only' forex CCP. solution.final_explanation:

solution.concept_anchor: PSS Act 2007 and settlement finality legal backing
solution.strong_distractor: a — Associating CCIL's legal framework with the 'Banking Regulation Act, 1949' is plausible because RBI regulates CCIL, and RBI's supervisory powers over banks derive from the BR Act — candidates may conflate the two.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Banking Regulation Act, 1949 governs the functioning of banks — it is not the statute that provides legal framework for payment and settlement systems or netting finality.
Eliminate option (b): The RBI Act, 1934 governs RBI's constitution and monetary policy functions — it does not specifically provide for settlement finality or legal recognition of netting.
Eliminate option (d): Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 governs securities markets under SEBI — it has no jurisdiction over CCIL's operations.

Confirm option (c): The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 specifically designates RBI as the authority for payment systems, authorises CCIL's settlement operations, and provides statutory backing for settlement finality and netting — making reversals impossible even in insolvency.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal and entity-swap trap combines two attractive wrong options: the BR Act (because RBI, which supervises banks, regulates CCIL) and the RBI Act (because it governs RBI itself). Both sound like plausible legal homes for CCIL's regulatory framework. The PSS Act, 2007, is a later, specific legislation — its precise year and purpose (payment systems, not banking or monetary policy in general) is the discriminator. Candidates who know RBI regulates CCIL but have not studied the specific statutory basis will choose option (a) or (b).
solution.final_explanation:
CCIL's legal mandate — including the finality of its settlement and the legal enforceability of its netting — rests on a specific statute.

• Option (a) — Banking Regulation Act, 1949: Governs banking companies and cooperative banks — does not provide for payment system authorisation or settlement finality. Incorrect.
• Option (b) — RBI Act, 1934: Governs RBI's constitution, monetary policy functions, and issue of currency — does not contain provisions specifically authorising payment systems or netting finality. Incorrect.
• Option (c) — Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007: Correct. This Act designates RBI as the authority for payment and settlement systems. CCIL operates as an 'authorised payment system' under this Act. Critically, the PSS Act provides statutory recognition to netting and settlement finality — once a transaction is settled through CCIL, it cannot be reversed even if a member subsequently becomes insolvent.
• Option (d) — SCRA, 1956: Governs securities contracts and markets, under SEBI's ambit — not applicable to CCIL's payment system functions. Incorrect.

Value Addition:
• Before the PSS Act 2007, netting agreements had legal vulnerability under insolvency law — a trustee in bankruptcy could potentially cherry-pick favourable trades.
• PSS Act Section 23 provides for finality of settlement — a cornerstone of systemic confidence in CCIL.
• The PSS Act also empowers RBI to designate and supervise payment system operators — CCIL's authorisation flows from this power.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Attributing the overnight rate spike to 'SEBI-imposed margin increases on equity derivatives' sounds plausible in a general financial stress scenario and exploits the confusion about which regulator controls which market.
elimination_logic: Identify the key scenario elements: tight liquidity conditions in the interbank money market → overnight rate spiking above the policy repo rate → concern for monetary policy transmission.
Recall that TREP (operated by CCIL) is the primary overnight collateralised money market — its rate reflects interbank liquidity conditions.

Evaluate option (d): The TREP rate spiking above the LAF repo rate signals tight liquidity, prompting RBI to inject funds through LAF operations — the scenario describes exactly this transmission channel where CCIL's TREP platform is the diagnostic tool and LAF is the response mechanism.
Eliminate option (a): CCIL calling additional margin is an intraday risk management tool for member-specific exposure — not the mechanism by which overnight rates spike.
Eliminate option (b): SEBI regulates equity derivatives margin — irrelevant to interbank G-Sec/money market overnight rates.
Eliminate option (c): CCIL does not determine the repo rate — RBI's MPC sets it. CCIL's TREP rate is a market-determined rate within the LAF corridor.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in option (a) is subtle: CCIL does collect margins, and margin calls do affect liquidity — but the connection described (CCIL's margin mechanism causing the overnight rate spike) confuses two different phenomena. Margin calls drain specific members' liquidity for specific positions; the TREP rate spike reflects system-wide overnight funding conditions. A candidate who knows CCIL collects margins may incorrectly link margin calls to overnight rate movements without seeing the institutional distinction.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the linkage between CCIL's TREP platform and RBI's monetary policy transmission framework.

**Applicable principle:** The TREP rate is the primary overnight interbank rate, anchored within RBI's LAF corridor (between SDF rate and repo rate). When system-wide liquidity tightens, the TREP rate rises toward the repo rate ceiling. RBI monitors TREP rate deviations from the policy rate as a signal for LAF operations — injecting or absorbing liquidity to keep rates within the corridor.

**Mapping to scenario:** A TREP rate spike above the repo rate signals excess demand for overnight liquidity. This is the diagnostic signal that triggers RBI's LAF repo operations — injecting funds into the banking system. The scenario describes CCIL's TREP platform as the transmission mechanism and diagnostic indicator for monetary policy operations.

• Option (a): Incorrect. CCIL's margin calls affect specific members' liquidity positions — they are not the mechanism by which system-wide overnight rates spike.
• Option (b): Incorrect. SEBI's equity derivative margin requirements are irrelevant to the interbank money market overnight rate.
• Option (c): Incorrect. CCIL does not set the repo rate — the MPC sets the policy repo rate. The TREP rate is market-determined within the LAF corridor.
• Option (d): Correct. The TREP rate signal of tight liquidity conditions triggers RBI's LAF repo injections — this is the textbook transmission channel.

Value Addition:
• When TREP rate = SDF rate → surplus liquidity; TREP rate → repo rate → tight liquidity.
• RBI uses variable-rate repos/reverse repos under LAF to manage TREP rate within the corridor.
• CCIL's TREP data is a real-time window into system liquidity — RBI's liquidity management desk monitors it closely.

solution.concept_anchor: QCCP capital treatment and default management distinction

statement_analysis.statement: Under Basel III norms, banks that clear trades through a QCCP are exempt from maintaining any capital against those exposures, since the CCP's guarantee eliminates all counterparty credit risk.
statement_analysis.reason: Basel III does not exempt banks from capital entirely — it assigns a preferentially low risk weight (typically 2%) to trade exposures against QCCPs. Capital must still be maintained, but at a significantly reduced rate compared to bilateral OTC trades.

statement_analysis.statement: When a CCIL member defaults, CCIL takes over the defaulting member's open positions and may manage them through hedging, auctioning, or close-out — without necessarily invoking the Settlement Guarantee Fund in every default scenario.
statement_analysis.reason: CCIL's default management involves position management (hedging, auctioning, close-out) as the first response. The SGF is invoked only if losses exceed the defaulting member's own margin and resources — not in every default scenario.

statement_analysis.statement: The distinction between initial margin (pre-funded by the specific defaulting member) and the default fund (pre-funded by all members collectively) is that initial margin is returned to a member once it closes its positions, while the default fund contribution is permanently forfeited upon joining CCIL.
statement_analysis.reason: Default fund contributions are not permanently forfeited — they are contributed by all members as a standing pool and are returned (or adjusted) when a member exits CCIL membership in good standing. Forfeiture occurs only upon a member's actual default, and even then, only to the extent of losses.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) claiming 'both 1 and 3' are incorrect is the correct answer but the distractor is option (d) — all three are incorrect — since Statement 1 has an obvious error (exemption vs. reduced weight) and Statement 3 also has an error, candidates may dismiss Statement 2 as well without careful reading.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: 'Exempt from maintaining any capital' is the scope-extension — Basel III assigns a low but non-zero risk weight (2%) to QCCP exposures, not zero. Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: CCIL managing defaulter's positions through hedging/auction before invoking SGF — accurate description of the default management process. Statement 2 is correct — do not select it as NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 3: Default fund contributions are not 'permanently forfeited' — they are a standing pool contribution, returned upon orderly exit. Permanent forfeiture on joining is factually wrong. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1's trap is the scope-extension from 'reduced capital' to 'no capital'. Basel III's preferential treatment for QCCPs is well-known, and candidates may round this to 'exempt' — especially because the 2% risk weight is so low compared to bilateral OTC exposures (which can attract 100%+ risk weights). Statement 3 exploits misunderstanding of default fund mechanics — the word 'permanently forfeited' is the insertion that makes the otherwise plausible statement incorrect. Both traps require precise knowledge of the quantitative and legal details, not just general awareness.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precision on two related risk management concepts: QCCP capital treatment and default fund mechanics.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: Basel III grants preferential but not zero capital treatment for QCCP exposures. Banks must hold capital at a 2% risk weight against trade exposures to QCCPs — significantly lower than bilateral OTC trades but not exempt. 'Exempt from maintaining any capital' overstates the benefit.
• Statement 2 — Correct: CCIL's default management hierarchy begins with position management — hedging open positions, auctioning them to solvent members, or closing out. The SGF is a backstop resource invoked only when position management losses exceed the defaulter's own resources.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: Default fund contributions are standing pool contributions maintained by members — they are not permanently forfeited upon joining. Members in good standing who exit CCIL are entitled to a return of their contribution. Forfeiture is triggered only upon an actual default, and even then proportionally.

Value Addition:
• The 2% risk weight for QCCP trade exposures under Basel III compares with 20–150% for bilateral OTC counterparties depending on their credit rating.
• Default fund contributions also attract a separate Basel III capital charge — calculated based on the hypothetical capital requirement (KCCP) of the CCP itself.
• Exit from CCIL membership requires regulatory approval and orderly unwinding of positions — it is not a simple withdrawal.

solution.strong_distractor: b — 'Only two' as the answer might attract candidates who are uncertain about Statement 4 (CCIL's forex role) and dismiss it as an overstatement, or who incorrectly accept Statement 3 based on CCIL's broad role perception.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: G-Sec settlement on NDS-OM — unambiguously a CCIL function. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: TREP replacing CBLO in November 2018 with CCIL as tri-party agent — documented and precise. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: 'Equity index futures on NSE' — this is NSE Clearing Ltd's domain under SEBI, not CCIL's. Incorrect.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the temporal-swap trap with an entity-swap layered on top: 'interest rate futures' sounds like it could be in CCIL's domain since CCIL handles interest rate instruments (G-Secs). But exchange-traded interest rate futures on NSE are derivatives products under SEBI's jurisdiction, cleared by NSE Clearing Ltd — not CCIL. The conflation of 'interest rate instrument' (CCIL's domain) with 'interest rate futures on an exchange' (SEBI's domain) is the precise knowledge test.
solution.final_explanation:
CCIL's operational mandate spans G-Secs, forex, and money markets — strictly within RBI's regulatory domain.

• Statement 1 — Correct: G-Sec clearing and settlement (outright and repo on NDS-OM) is CCIL's foundational function, providing DvP-III-based guaranteed settlement.

• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Equity index futures and exchange-traded interest rate futures on NSE are cleared by NSE Clearing Ltd under SEBI. CCIL has no role in exchange-traded derivatives regardless of the underlying asset class.
• Statement 4 — Correct: CCIL is India's sole onshore CCP for the USD/INR forex market — covering spot, forward, and swap segments with full settlement guarantee, addressing Herstatt risk for the INR leg.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) swaps the Trade Repository function with the Securities Settlement System description, exploiting the surface similarity between 'collecting and maintaining records' (TR) and 'record of G-Sec ownership' (SGL/SSS). Candidates may conflate these.
elimination_logic: Identify A: CCP role — CCIL interposes itself as buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer — matches '3: Interposes itself as buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer through novation'.

Identify B: Securities Settlement System — CCIL settles G-Sec transactions using DvP; the actual G-Sec ownership record is in RBI's SGL — matches '1: Settles G-Sec transactions on DvP basis; actual ownership records maintained in RBI's SGL'.

Identify C: Trade Repository — collects OTC derivative transaction data for RBI's regulatory use — matches '4: Collects and maintains records of OTC derivative transactions for regulatory surveillance'.

Identify D: Tri-party agent in TREP — manages collateral selection, valuation, transfer, substitution on behalf of parties — matches '2: Manages collateral selection, valuation, and substitution on behalf of borrowers and lenders'. Correct matching: option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap is between 'Securities Settlement System' (B) and 'Trade Repository' (C). Both involve record-keeping and data management. SSS records G-Sec transaction settlements (working with RBI's SGL for actual ownership), while TR collects OTC derivative transaction data for regulatory use. Option (b) swaps these two, assigning TR's description ('collecting records of derivative transactions') to SSS and SSS's description to TR. The key discriminator is 'G-Sec settlement records' (SSS/SGL) versus 'OTC derivative transaction records' (TR).
solution.final_explanation:
CCIL performs multiple distinct institutional roles in India's financial infrastructure.

**Correct matches:**
• A–3 (Central Counterparty/CCP): CCIL's defining identity — through novation, it becomes the legal counterparty to every cleared trade, eliminating bilateral counterparty risk. This applies across G-Secs, forex, and money market segments.
• B–1 (Securities Settlement System): CCIL operates the SSS for G-Secs, settling transactions on a DvP-III basis. The actual ownership registry for G-Secs is maintained in RBI's SGL — CCIL orchestrates the settlement, SGL records the title change.
• C–4 (Trade Repository): CCIL's TR collects, stores, and reports OTC derivative transaction data (interest rate swaps, forex derivatives). Banks are mandated by RBI to report all OTC derivative trades here. Regulators use this data for systemic risk surveillance.
• D–2 (Tri-Party Agent in TREP): In the TREP platform, CCIL acts as tri-party agent — selecting eligible collateral, valuing it daily, arranging transfer, and managing substitutions on behalf of borrower and lender.

Value Addition:
• CCIL thus wears four distinct hats: CCP (risk absorber), SSS (settlement operator), TR (data repository), and tri-party agent (collateral manager).
• Each function is operationally segregated — losses in one do not cross-contaminate others.
• CCIL's TR function is India's designated OTC derivative data repository under RBI's regulatory framework.

statement_analysis.statement: CCIL's designation as a Systemically Important Financial Market Infrastructure (SIFMI) by RBI means it is assessed against all 24 CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures.
statement_analysis.reason: SIFMI designation subjects CCIL to enhanced regulatory assessment, including RBI's evaluation of CCIL's compliance with all 24 CPMI-IOSCO PFMIs covering governance, risk management, settlement, and operational resilience.

statement_analysis.statement: Recovery and Resolution Planning (RRP) for CCIL means that CCIL itself prepares a recovery plan while an external authority (RBI) would execute a resolution plan in case recovery fails — the two plans are legally distinct.
statement_analysis.reason: Recovery is CCIL's own plan to survive extreme stress using its own tools (margin haircutting, partial tear-up, etc.); resolution is an externally-administered process if recovery fails — these are legally and operationally distinct frameworks.

statement_analysis.statement: The SIFMI designation ensures that CCIL will always be rescued by the Indian government if it faces insolvency, as the government has a statutory obligation to provide financial support to SIFMIs.
statement_analysis.reason: There is no statutory obligation for government rescue of SIFMIs — the 'too important to fail' characterisation refers to the systemic consequences of failure, not a government guarantee. RRP frameworks are specifically designed so that resolution tools (not government bailouts) address SIFMI failures.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All three correct' exploits the 'too important to fail' rhetoric: candidates who associate systemic importance with implicit government guarantees (as in 'too big to fail' banks) may accept Statement 3 as correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: CPMI-IOSCO PFMI assessment by RBI for SIFMI-designated entities — this is the standard regulatory practice. Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Recovery (CCIL's own tools) vs. Resolution (external authority's process) — the two-stage, legally distinct framework. Correct.

Evaluate Statement 3: 'Statutory obligation to rescue' — no such obligation exists. SIFMI designation enhances oversight and requires RRP, but does not create a government guarantee. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the conflation of 'systemic importance' with 'implicit government guarantee'. The 'too big to fail' narrative surrounding global systemically important banks (G-SIBs) has created an association between systemic importance and government rescue. SIFMI designation is precisely the opposite in intent — it mandates RRP to ensure that systemic FMIs can be resolved without government bailout. The word 'statutory obligation' is the scope-extension that makes Statement 3 definitively incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
CCIL's SIFMI designation is about enhanced oversight and crisis preparedness — not a government guarantee.

• Statement 1 — Correct: RBI assesses CCIL against all 24 CPMI-IOSCO PFMIs — covering governance, credit risk, liquidity risk, collateral, margin, settlement finality, default management, operational resilience, and disclosure. This is a rigorous annual exercise.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Recovery and Resolution Planning has two legally distinct components. Recovery Plan: CCIL's own plan using tools like variation margin haircutting, partial contract tear-up, and capital calls to survive extreme stress while remaining open. Resolution Plan: If recovery tools are exhausted, RBI (as the resolution authority) would administer an externally controlled process to wind down or restructure CCIL.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: SIFMI designation creates no statutory government rescue obligation. The entire logic of SIFMI regulation is to design pre-funded private sector buffers (SGF, default fund, CCIL capital) so that systemic FMIs can be resolved without public funds. Post-2008 crisis regulatory reform explicitly moved away from implicit government guarantees.

Value Addition:
• Global precedent: The 2012 BIS report 'Recovery and Resolution of Financial Market Infrastructures' established the international framework for CCP RRP.
• Recovery tools for CCPs include: partial tear-up (cancelling contracts to restore balance), VMGH (variation margin gain haircutting), and cash calls from non-defaulting members.
• India's SIFMI framework is aligned with FSB (Financial Stability Board) guidance on FMI resolution — making CCIL's RRP internationally comparable.

solution.concept_anchor: RBI Retail Direct and CCIL indirect infrastructure role

statement_analysis.statement: Under RBI's Retail Direct Scheme, individual investors can purchase Central Government securities directly from RBI — this makes them direct members of CCIL, bypassing the traditional bank-intermediated settlement path.
statement_analysis.reason: RBI Retail Direct allows individuals to buy G-Secs directly from RBI through a gilt account, but this does not confer CCIL membership. Settlement for retail direct investors flows through the CCIL-supported infrastructure via member intermediaries — retail investors are not and cannot be direct CCIL members.

statement_analysis.statement: CCIL's role in the interbank money market — particularly through the TREP platform — is relevant to monetary policy transmission because the TREP rate is anchored within RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) interest rate corridor.
statement_analysis.reason: TREP is the primary overnight collateralised money market, and its rate reflects prevailing liquidity conditions within the LAF corridor. The link between TREP rate and the LAF repo/SDF rates is the transmission channel for monetary policy signals.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Both statements appearing correct is tempting: Statement 1 partially sounds right because Retail Direct does involve RBI's infrastructure directly, and Statement 2 is clearly correct. The partial-truth in Statement 1 is the trap.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: 'Makes them direct members of CCIL' is the critical error — Retail Direct provides G-Sec access through RBI, but CCIL membership requires regulated institutional status. Individuals cannot be CCIL members. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: TREP rate anchored within LAF corridor → monetary policy transmission channel — accurately described. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect + Statement 2 correct → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a partial-truth: the Retail Direct Scheme does involve RBI's infrastructure and does allow direct G-Sec access — both of which are true. The false element is 'makes them direct members of CCIL'. The scheme bypasses traditional bank intermediation for purchase but not for the settlement infrastructure — settlement still flows through CCIL-member banks' channels. A candidate who knows Retail Direct is a 'direct' scheme may interpret 'direct' as extending to CCIL membership, which it does not.
solution.final_explanation:
These two statements test the boundary between retail G-Sec access mechanisms and CCIL's wholesale institutional structure.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: RBI's Retail Direct Scheme (launched November 2021) enables individual investors to open Retail Direct Gilt Accounts with RBI and purchase G-Secs directly in primary auctions and secondary markets. However, 'direct' here refers to the relationship between the investor and RBI for transaction purposes — not CCIL membership. Settlement continues to flow through CCIL's infrastructure via member institutions. CCIL membership is restricted to regulated wholesale institutions — banks, primary dealers, insurance companies. Retail investors remain outside this structure.
• Statement 2 — Correct: TREP (operated by CCIL) is the dominant overnight money market rate indicator. Its weighted average rate trades within the LAF corridor — between the SDF rate (floor) and the repo rate (ceiling). When the TREP rate deviates from the policy midpoint, it signals liquidity tightness or surplus, triggering RBI's LAF operations.

Value Addition:
• RBI Retail Direct Scheme: Investors open a 'Retail Direct Gilt Account' with RBI — analogous to a demat account but for G-Secs, maintained by RBI.
• The settlement of Retail Direct transactions is facilitated through the NDS-OM-linked infrastructure where CCIL provides the settlement guarantee — but the retail investor interacts only with RBI, not CCIL.
• TREP rate is the Indian equivalent of the US federal funds rate as an overnight interbank liquidity indicator.
